title: Eschatology and Cosmic Cycles: Ragnarok, Pralaya, and the End of the World Across Traditions
description: A comparative study of eschatological and cosmological cycle traditions across five major civilizations: Norse (Ragnarok), Vedic-Hindu (Pralaya and the Yuga system), Buddhist (Kalpas), Greek (Hesiod's Ages of Man and Stoic Ekpyrosis), and Aztec (Five Suns). Each tradition envisions cosmic destruction and potential renewal, but with profoundly different theological implications -- from the irreversible entropy of the Greek Ages to the mathematically precise cyclic time of Hindu cosmology to the sacrificial maintenance of the Aztec cosmos. This analysis examines the deep structural parallels while honoring the distinct metaphysical commitments of each tradition.

theoretical_framework.linear_vs_cyclic: A fundamental distinction in comparative eschatology is between linear time (a single creation moving toward a final end, as in Abrahamic traditions) and cyclic time (endless repetition of creation and destruction, as in Hindu and Buddhist cosmology). Norse and Greek traditions occupy an interesting middle position: cyclic in structure but with unique events in each cycle.
theoretical_framework.entropy_vs_renewal: Some traditions emphasize progressive degeneration (Greek Ages decline from Gold to Iron; Hindu Yugas decline from Satya to Kali), while others emphasize renewal (Norse Ragnarok leads to a green earth; the Aztec creation of each new Sun). Buddhism uniquely combines both: kalpas cycle endlessly, but individual liberation (nirvana) offers escape from the cycle entirely.
key_scholars: Mircea Eliade, 'The Myth of the Eternal Return' (1954) -- foundational analysis of cyclic time in archaic religions
Lincoln, Bruce, 'Death, War, and Sacrifice' (1991) -- Indo-European eschatological parallels
Maffie, James, 'Aztec Philosophy' (2014) -- Nahua metaphysics of motion and transformation

cycles.name: Ragnarok (Old Norse: Ragnarokr, 'Fate of the Gods' or Ragnarkkr, 'Twilight of the Gods')
cycles.source_text: Voluspa (Poetic Edda, c. 10th century CE), Prose Edda Gylfaginning (Snorri Sturluson, c. 1220 CE), Vafthrudnismal
cycles.cosmological_context: Norse cosmology posits a world-tree (Yggdrasil) connecting nine worlds, created from the body of the primordial giant Ymir. The cosmos is sustained by the tension between the gods (Aesir and Vanir) and the forces of chaos (giants, Loki, the Midgard Serpent). Ragnarok is the inevitable resolution of this tension.
cycles.trigger: A cascading series of portents: the Fimbulvetr (Great Winter) lasting three years with no intervening summer; the dissolution of all moral bonds (brothers killing brothers, kin-ties broken); the breaking of Fenrir's chain Gleipnir; Loki freed from his punishment beneath the serpent. The cock Fjalar crows in Jotunheim, Gullinkambi crows in Asgard, and a rust-red rooster crows in Hel. These events signal the irreversible unraveling of the cosmic order that the gods had maintained since the binding of the great monsters.
cycles.destruction: The forces of chaos converge: the wolf Fenrir swallows the sun; the Midgard Serpent Jormungandr rises from the ocean, poisoning the sky; the fire giant Surt advances from Muspelheim with his flaming sword; the ship Naglfar (made from dead men's fingernails) carries the armies of Hel; Loki leads the forces of chaos. The gods march to battle on the plain of Vigrid. In the final combat: Odin is swallowed by Fenrir; Thor slays Jormungandr but dies from its venom after nine steps; Freyr falls to Surt (having given away his invincible sword to win Gerd); Tyr and the hound Garm kill each other; Heimdall and Loki slay each other. Surt engulfs the world in fire. The earth sinks into the sea.
cycles.survivors: Vidar (Odin's son) avenges his father by tearing Fenrir's jaws apart. Modi and Magni (Thor's sons) survive and inherit Mjolnir. Baldr and Hodr return from Hel, reconciled. The human couple Lif and Lifthrasir survive hidden in the wood Hoddmimis Holt (or within Yggdrasil itself), nourished by morning dew. A new sun, daughter of the old one, takes the sky-path.
cycles.renewal: The earth rises again from the sea, green and fair. Unsown fields bear fruit. The surviving gods gather on the renewed Idavoll plain and find the golden chess-pieces of the old gods in the grass. A great hall, Gimle, more beautiful than the sun, shelters the righteous. The Voluspa's final stanzas describe a mysterious 'mighty one' who comes from above to rule -- possibly a Christian interpolation or a genuine Norse concept of a supreme deity beyond the Aesir. The new world corrects the moral failures of the old: Baldr's return symbolizes innocence restored.
cycles.time_scale: Ragnarok is a singular event within a possibly cyclic framework. The Voluspa implies one complete cycle (creation from Ymir -> Ragnarok -> renewal), but does not explicitly state that the cycle repeats. Some scholars (Lindow 2001) argue the cyclic element is structural but not necessarily infinite as in Hindu cosmology. The Fimbulvetr is three years; the battle itself appears to occur in a single cataclysmic day.
cycles.philosophical_significance: Ragnarok embodies the uniquely Norse (and broadly Germanic) tragic heroism: the gods know they will lose and fight anyway. Odin's entire existence is preparation for a battle he knows he will not survive. This stands in stark contrast to the Hindu divine play (lila) or the Aztec sacrificial maintenance of the cosmos. Ragnarok also functions as a theodicy: the moral decay that triggers it explains evil as the breakdown of cosmic bonds, while the renewal promises that destruction is not final. The theme of the gods' moral culpability (their broken oaths, their treatment of Loki) introduces a dimension of divine accountability absent from most eschatologies.

cycles.name: Pralaya (Sanskrit: dissolution) within the Yuga Cycle and Brahma's Cosmic Day
cycles.source_text: Vishnu Purana (c. 4th-5th century CE), Bhagavata Purana, Mahabharata (Markandeya's account), Matsya Purana (Flood narrative), Laws of Manu, Surya Siddhanta (astronomical calculations)
cycles.cosmological_context: Hindu cosmology operates on multiple nested time scales of staggering magnitude. The basic unit is the Yuga cycle (Chatur-Yuga or Maha-Yuga), comprising four ages of declining dharma. These aggregate into the Day and Night of Brahma (Kalpa), which aggregate into Brahma's life of 100 divine years. The entire system is infinite: when one Brahma dies, another arises. This is the most mathematically elaborated cosmological time system in any pre-modern civilization.
cycles.trigger: Pralaya occurs at multiple scales: (1) Naimittika Pralaya (incidental dissolution) at the end of each Kalpa (Day of Brahma), when Brahma sleeps. (2) Prakritika Pralaya (elemental dissolution) at the end of Brahma's life, when all matter dissolves back into Prakriti. (3) Atyantika Pralaya (absolute dissolution) -- the liberation (moksha) of an individual soul from the cycle, not a cosmic event. (4) Nitya Pralaya (constant dissolution) -- the continuous cycle of death and rebirth in all beings. The trigger for cosmic Pralaya is the exhaustion of a cosmic time period, often accompanied by the decline of dharma to its nadir. At the end of the Kali Yuga, Vishnu incarnates as Kalki to destroy the wicked and reset the cycle.
cycles.destruction: The Vishnu Purana describes the end-of-Kalpa Pralaya: seven suns appear in the sky and drink up the oceans; fire consumes the earth; tremendous winds arise; torrential rains fall for a hundred divine years, flooding everything; Brahma (as Narayana/Vishnu) sleeps on the cosmic serpent Shesha upon the waters of dissolution, and the entire universe exists in potentia within his divine body. At the Prakritika Pralaya (end of Brahma's life): earth dissolves into water, water into fire, fire into wind, wind into space, space into ego (ahamkara), ego into mahat (cosmic intelligence), and mahat dissolves back into the unmanifest Prakriti -- a precise reversal of the Samkhya cosmogonic sequence.
cycles.survivors: At the Naimittika Pralaya, Brahma himself survives (he sleeps). The Saptarishi (Seven Sages) and Manu are preserved to repopulate the next cycle, often through a flood narrative (the Matsya Avatara, where Vishnu as a fish guides Manu's boat through the deluge). Seeds, Vedic knowledge, and dharmic principles are preserved in potentia. At the Prakritika Pralaya, only the Absolute (Brahman/Vishnu/Shiva depending on sectarian orientation) persists -- all else dissolves.
cycles.renewal: Brahma awakens and re-creates the universe through tapas (cosmic heat/meditation), re-emanating the elements in sequence. A new Satya Yuga (Golden Age) begins with dharma at full strength. The Vedas are re-revealed (or remembered by the surviving sages). The cycle is identical in structure but not necessarily in detail -- each Kalpa has its own specific narratives, avatars, and events. The renewal is not 'progress' but oscillation: dharma will inevitably decline again through the four Yugas.
cycles.time_scale: Satya Yuga: 1,728,000 years. Treta Yuga: 1,296,000 years. Dvapara Yuga: 864,000 years. Kali Yuga: 432,000 years. One Maha-Yuga (Chatur-Yuga): 4,320,000 years. One Kalpa (Day of Brahma): 1,000 Maha-Yugas = 4,320,000,000 years. Brahma's Night: equal duration. Brahma's full life: 311.04 trillion years. Current position: we are in the Kali Yuga of the 28th Maha-Yuga of the Vaivasvata Manvantara (7th of 14) in the Shveta-Varaha Kalpa, in the 51st year of the current Brahma's life.
cycles.philosophical_significance: The Hindu Pralaya system represents the most radical expression of cyclic time in world religion. Its philosophical import is twofold: (1) it relativizes all human and even divine history -- the gods themselves are subject to the cycle, and Brahma dies -- rendering all worldly achievement ultimately provisional; (2) it elevates moksha (liberation from the cycle) as the supreme goal, since no amount of cyclic existence can provide permanent satisfaction. The system also served practical astronomical purposes: the Surya Siddhanta uses Yuga periods as a framework for calculating planetary positions. The scale dwarfs all other cosmological time systems, predating modern cosmology's comparable scales (the age of the universe at 13.8 billion years is roughly three Brahma-days).

cycles.name: Kappa/Kalpa (Pali/Sanskrit: aeon) -- the Cosmic Cycle of Arising and Dissolution
cycles.source_text: Agganna Sutta (Digha Nikaya 27), Visuddhimagga (Buddhaghosa, 5th century CE), Abhidharmakosa (Vasubandhu, 4th-5th century CE), Lotus Sutra (Mahayana)
cycles.cosmological_context: Buddhist cosmology inherits and transforms the Indian Kalpa system within a framework that denies a creator deity and emphasizes dependent origination (pratityasamutpada). The cosmos arises and dissolves through the collective karma of sentient beings, not through divine will. There is no first beginning -- the cycle of samsara is beginningless (anamatagga). The cosmos is structured vertically into desire realm, form realm, and formless realm, with multiple world-systems (lokadhatu) existing simultaneously.
cycles.trigger: Destruction occurs through three possible agents, cycling in a fixed pattern: fire (destroying up to the first jhana heaven of the form realm), water (destroying up to the second jhana heaven), and wind (destroying up to the third jhana heaven). The fourth jhana heaven is never destroyed. The trigger is not divine wrath but the maturation of collective karma and the natural exhaustion of the world-system's sustaining conditions. Before the destruction, beings gradually migrate to higher realms; no being is destroyed in the catastrophe because all have already departed through karmic processes.
cycles.destruction: In fire-destruction (the most commonly described): seven suns appear successively, each more terrible than the last. The first dries up small streams; the second dries rivers; the third dries the great lakes; the fourth dries the ocean; the fifth and sixth consume the earth; the seventh blazes with cosmic fire that destroys everything up to the Brahma realms. In water-destruction: caustic rains dissolve all material existence. In wind-destruction: cosmic gales tear apart all structures. The destruction phase (samvattakappa) lasts as long as the formation phase -- an incalculable number of years. During the period of dissolution, 'empty space' persists.
cycles.survivors: No beings 'survive' in the physical sense; rather, all sentient beings have already been reborn in higher realms (the Abhassara/Abhasvara heaven for fire-destruction) before the lower realms are destroyed. When the world re-forms, beings from the higher realms, their merit exhausted, 'fall' back down and repopulate the lower realms. The Agganna Sutta describes this process with remarkable psychological insight: beings taste the 'earth-essence' (a sweet substance on the newly formed earth), become attached to it, and gradually develop denser bodies, gender differentiation, agriculture, property, and social hierarchy -- a Buddhist 'fall' narrative driven by craving (tanha) rather than divine punishment.
cycles.renewal: The world re-forms (vivattakappa) through natural processes. First, rain falls into the void; a wind arises and supports the water; the water solidifies into earth. The cosmos reconstitutes in reverse order of its destruction. Beings descend from higher realms. The process is described with quasi-scientific detachment: no creator deity intervenes; the cosmos self-organizes through the interplay of elemental forces and collective karma. Each new world-system has its own Buddhas who rediscover and teach the Dharma.
cycles.time_scale: A Maha-Kalpa consists of four phases: formation (vivattakappa), stability (vivattatthayi), dissolution (samvattakappa), and emptiness (samvattatthayi), each lasting an 'incalculable' (asamkhyeya) number of years. The Buddha illustrated the length of a kalpa with parables: a kalpa is longer than the time it would take to wear down a mountain of solid granite, one cubic yojana in size, by brushing it once every hundred years with a fine silk cloth. A Maha-Kalpa encompasses four such periods. The number of past Maha-Kalpas is infinite; there is no first kalpa.
cycles.philosophical_significance: Buddhist eschatology is unique in several respects: (1) There is no creator and no eschatological judge -- the cosmos arises and dissolves through impersonal karmic processes. (2) Cosmic time is explicitly declared to be beginningless and endless, with no possibility of a 'final' end. (3) The purpose of contemplating cosmic time is not cosmological curiosity but the generation of samvega (spiritual urgency): recognizing the vast scale of samsaric suffering motivates the practitioner to seek liberation. (4) The Buddhist cosmos is radically plural: infinite world-systems exist simultaneously, each with its own cycle. (5) Uniquely, Buddhism offers an 'escape clause' from the cycle: nirvana is the cessation of the individual's participation in samsara, achieved through the Noble Eightfold Path, regardless of the cosmic cycle's phase.

cycles.name: The Ages of Man (Hesiod) and Stoic Ekpyrosis
cycles.source_text: Hesiod, Works and Days (c. 700 BCE), lines 106-201; Ovid, Metamorphoses 1.89-150 (Roman adaptation); Stoic fragments (Chrysippus, Cleanthes, preserved in Diogenes Laertius and Stobaeus)
cycles.cosmological_context: Greek eschatology presents two distinct traditions: (1) Hesiod's myth of the Five Ages (Gold, Silver, Bronze, Heroic, Iron), representing progressive degeneration of the human condition; and (2) the Stoic doctrine of Ekpyrosis, a cyclic conflagration and renewal of the cosmos. These represent two fundamentally different cosmological orientations -- entropic decline versus eternal recurrence -- that coexisted in ancient Greek thought.
cycles.trigger: In Hesiod: the decline is moral and ontological. Zeus creates each successive race; each is inferior to the last (with the anomalous insertion of the Heroic Age between Bronze and Iron). The trigger for each age's end is the moral failure of its inhabitants: the Silver race refused to honor the gods; the Bronze race destroyed each other through violence; the Iron race will end when babies are born with grey hair and shame and justice abandon the earth. In Stoic Ekpyrosis: the cosmos reaches a state of maximum dryness (pneuma at its most active), and the divine fire (the creative logos-fire, not destructive fire) reabsorbs all matter into itself. This is not destruction but the cosmos returning to its purest state.
cycles.destruction: Hesiod does not describe the physical destruction of each age but rather the replacement of one race by another -- a moral/genealogical scheme rather than a cosmological one. The Iron Age will end when Aidos (Shame) and Nemesis (Righteous Indignation) abandon humanity, wrapping themselves in white robes and departing for Olympus. Ovid's version adds a physical flood (Deucalion's flood, parallel to Noah and Manu) at the transition from the Bronze/Iron Age. Stoic Ekpyrosis involves the entire cosmos being consumed by divine fire and returning to the state of pure creative reason (logos spermatikos). Chrysippus argued this was not destruction but purification -- the cosmos as a living being undergoing a natural cycle of expiration and respiration.
cycles.survivors: In Hesiod: each age's race is replaced by a new creation; the Gold race become daimones (benevolent spirits); the Silver become blessed spirits of the underworld; the Heroic go to the Isles of the Blessed. There is no continuity between ages -- each is a fresh creation by Zeus. In the Deucalion myth: Deucalion and Pyrrha survive the flood in an ark (or chest), repopulate the earth by throwing 'the bones of their mother' (stones) over their shoulders. In Stoic Ekpyrosis: Zeus/Logos alone persists through the conflagration. All individual souls are reabsorbed into the divine fire.
cycles.renewal: Hesiod is ambiguous about renewal: the Iron Age is the present, and its end appears final rather than cyclic (though some scholars detect a cyclical implication). Stoic cosmology is explicitly cyclic: after Ekpyrosis, the cosmos re-emerges (diakosmesis) in exactly the same form. Chrysippus argued that in each new cycle, the same events recur identically -- the same Socrates will drink the same hemlock. This doctrine of eternal recurrence (later adopted by Nietzsche) is the most radical form of cyclic cosmology in the Western tradition, exceeding even Hindu cyclicism in its insistence on exact repetition.
cycles.time_scale: Hesiod does not provide specific durations for the Ages. The Stoic Great Year (Magnus Annus) was variously calculated: some Stoics proposed 10,800 years (based on astronomical calculations of planetary return to identical positions); others proposed much longer periods. The concept of the Great Year was shared with Plato (Timaeus 39d) and Babylonian astronomical traditions. Compared to Hindu time scales, Greek cosmic time is modest.
cycles.philosophical_significance: Hesiod's Ages represent the earliest systematic articulation of the 'decline narrative' in Western thought -- the conviction that the past was better and the present represents a fall from primordial perfection. This profoundly influenced Western eschatology, from biblical Eden to Rousseau's noble savage. The Stoic Ekpyrosis represents the most sophisticated ancient attempt to reconcile a rational, deterministic cosmos with the observable reality of change and decay: if the cosmos is governed by perfect reason (logos), then it must repeat itself perfectly. The divergence between Hesiodic decline and Stoic eternal recurrence maps onto a fundamental tension in Greek thought between tragic pessimism and philosophical optimism.

cycles.name: The Five Suns (Nahui Ollin -- 'Four Movement', the current and final Sun)
cycles.source_text: Leyenda de los Soles (Legend of the Suns, c. 1558); Codex Chimalpopoca; Historia de los Mexicanos por sus Pinturas; Codex Vaticanus A/Rios; Bernardino de Sahagun, Florentine Codex (Book 7)
cycles.cosmological_context: Aztec cosmology posits a series of world ages, each presided over by a different Sun (deity) and destroyed by a specific cataclysm. The current Fifth Sun was created through divine self-sacrifice at Teotihuacan. The cosmos is maintained not by divine fiat but by continuous reciprocal sacrifice between gods and humans -- if sacrifice ceases, the Sun will stop moving and the world will end. This 'maintenance cosmology' differs radically from both the entropic Greek model and the automatic cycling of Hindu-Buddhist systems.
cycles.trigger: Each Sun is destroyed because of conflict among the gods (particularly between Quetzalcoatl and Tezcatlipoca, whose rivalry drives cosmic history) and because each age's dominant beings prove inadequate. The First Sun (Nahui Ocelotl, Four Jaguar) ended when Tezcatlipoca was knocked from the sky and became a jaguar that devoured the giants. The Second Sun (Nahui Ehecatl, Four Wind) ended when Quetzalcoatl sent a great wind that destroyed everything and transformed the people into monkeys. The Third Sun (Nahui Quiahuitl, Four Rain) ended in a rain of fire. The Fourth Sun (Nahui Atl, Four Water) ended in a great flood lasting 52 years, transforming people into fish. The Fifth Sun (Nahui Ollin, Four Movement) will end through earthquakes and the descent of the Tzitzimimeh (skeletal star-demons).
cycles.destruction: Each destruction is total for its world-age: the beings of that age are transformed or annihilated, and the Sun itself ceases. The destruction is always associated with one of the four elements (earth/jaguar, wind, fire, water) plus the fifth (movement/earthquake for the current age). The current Fifth Sun is explicitly prophesied to end through earthquakes (ollin = movement). The Tzitzimimeh -- terrifying skeletal celestial beings associated with eclipses and the darkness between world-ages -- will descend and devour humanity. Every 52-year cycle (the New Fire ceremony, Toxiuhmolpilia), the Aztecs feared the Fifth Sun might end; the ceremony of drilling new fire on a sacrificial victim's chest was performed to ensure the Sun's continuation.
cycles.survivors: In most accounts, a single human couple survives each cataclysm through divine intervention. After the Fourth Sun's flood, Tata and Nene survived in a hollow cypress tree (ordered by Tezcatlipoca). They cooked fish over a fire, angering the gods with the smoke, and were transformed into dogs as punishment -- only partially surviving. The Fifth Sun's creation at Teotihuacan required the self-immolation of the humble god Nanahuatzin (who leaped into the fire to become the Sun) while the proud god Tecuciztecatl hesitated and became the Moon. The other gods then sacrificed themselves so that the Sun would move -- establishing the paradigm that sacrifice is the engine of cosmic motion.
cycles.renewal: Renewal is not automatic but requires divine sacrifice. The creation of the Fifth Sun at Teotihuacan is the paradigmatic act: the gods gather, build a great fire, and one must leap in to become the new Sun. Nanahuatzin's self-sacrifice is the foundational act that the Aztec sacrificial system ritually reenacts. The Sun initially refuses to move; only when Ehecatl (Quetzalcoatl as wind) sacrifices the other gods does the Sun begin its daily journey. Human sacrifice continues this cosmic maintenance: the hearts and blood offered to Huitzilopochtli (the tribal Sun-god of the Mexica) and Tonatiuh (the Sun) literally fuel the Sun's motion. Renewal is thus contingent, precarious, and demands perpetual human participation.
cycles.time_scale: Each Sun lasts a different period, generally measured in 52-year cycles (the xiuhmolpilli). The Leyenda de los Soles gives: First Sun: 676 years (13 x 52). Second Sun: 364 years (7 x 52). Third Sun: 312 years (6 x 52). Fourth Sun: 676 years (13 x 52). The Fifth Sun's duration is not fixed -- it depends on the continuation of sacrifice. The 52-year cycle is based on the coincidence of the 365-day solar calendar (xiuhpohualli) and the 260-day ritual calendar (tonalpohualli), which realign every 52 years.
cycles.philosophical_significance: The Aztec Five Suns system represents a unique eschatological model: the cosmos is neither automatically cyclic (as in Hindu-Buddhist thought) nor linearly declining (as in Hesiod) but actively maintained through reciprocal sacrifice. The philosophical implications are profound: (1) Cosmic order is fragile and contingent, not guaranteed by divine power or natural law. (2) Human beings are not passive recipients of divine dispensation but active co-creators of cosmic continuity. (3) Sacrifice is not appeasement of angry gods but the fundamental mechanism of cosmic motion -- teotl (divine power/sacred energy) must flow continuously between gods, humans, and the natural world. (4) As Maffie (2014) argues, Nahua metaphysics is processual rather than substantial: the cosmos is not a collection of things but an ongoing process of transformation (nepantla) requiring constant energetic input. This makes Aztec cosmology arguably the most existentially demanding of all world eschatologies.

structural_parallels: All five traditions envision cosmic destruction by elemental forces: fire (Surt in Norse, Stoic Ekpyrosis, the third Aztec Sun, the seven suns of Buddhist and Hindu dissolution), water (Deucalion, Manu's flood, the fourth Aztec Sun, Buddhist water-dissolution), wind (Aztec second Sun, Buddhist wind-dissolution), and earth (earthquake in Aztec fifth Sun).

All traditions except perhaps Hesiod include a flood narrative with survivors in a vessel or shelter (Lif and Lifthrasir, Manu, Deucalion, Tata and Nene), suggesting either a common mythological heritage or independent responses to actual catastrophic flooding in human memory.

A pattern of moral decline precedes destruction in multiple traditions: the Iron Age's moral collapse in Hesiod, the decay of dharma through the Yugas in Hinduism, the breakdown of social bonds before Ragnarok in Norse tradition.

The motif of cosmic fire as the ultimate purifier/destroyer appears in Norse (Surt), Stoic (Ekpyrosis), Hindu (the seven suns of Pralaya), Buddhist (fire-destruction kalpa), and Aztec (third Sun) traditions.
fundamental_differences: Agency: Norse gods fight and die heroically but cannot prevent Ragnarok; Hindu dissolution is the natural 'breathing' of Brahma; Buddhist dissolution arises from impersonal karmic forces; Aztec destruction results from divine conflict and requires active human maintenance to prevent.

Moral valence: Greek Ages are purely degenerative with no clear renewal; Norse Ragnarok combines catastrophe with hope (Baldr's return); Hindu Pralaya is morally neutral (a cosmic rhythm); Buddhist dissolution generates spiritual urgency; Aztec cosmic endings are transformative rather than purely destructive.

Time scale: Aztec Suns span centuries; Norse Ragnarok is a singular event; Greek Ages are unquantified; Buddhist Kalpas are 'incalculable'; Hindu Brahma-days span billions of years. Only the Hindu-Buddhist systems approach modern cosmological timescales.

Escapability: Only Buddhism offers an 'exit' from the cosmic cycle (nirvana/moksha). Norse heroes face inescapable fate (wyrd). Aztec humans are bound to sacrificial maintenance. Hindu liberation (moksha) parallels the Buddhist escape. Greek thought offers philosophical consolation (Stoic apatheia) but no escape from cosmic repetition.
comparative_synthesis.indo_european_connections: Lincoln (1991) and others have argued that Ragnarok and certain Vedic eschatological themes share a common PIE origin: the final battle (devas vs asuras / Aesir vs giants), the cosmic fire, the flood, and the renewal with surviving divine figures. The 'battle at the end of the world' may be a PIE mytheme, with the Greek Titanomachy/Gigantomachy as a displaced version (placed at the beginning of the current order rather than at its end).
